To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

electron addition at nanocrystallite SnO2 and TiO2 surfaces is accompanied by charge-compensating proton uptake, and that the proton uptake process is driven by water, rather than by hydronium ion, and is therefore a general mode of electron addition at metal oxide semiconductor surfaces.

(1) electron addition to nanocrystallline metal oxides in aqueous electrolyte is accompanied by protonation of the oxide surface, and (2) the resulting surface charge can be neutralized by counterion uptake.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the chemical and electrochemical properties of metal oxides.
the development of new materials and new methods for the production of hydrogen from water.
the development of novel materials for use in energy conversion and storage devices and with the understanding of their fundamental electronic and chemical properties.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the new results establish that electron addition at metal oxide semiconductor electrodes can be charge compensated by proton intercalation and/or adsorption.

the new results establish that the electrochemical reduction of SnO2 and of ZnO in aqueous media occurs via a mechanism in which electrons are added to the conduction band of the oxide, and that the concomitant charge compensation occurs by the uptake of protons from the electrolyte.
the new results are a significant advance in our understanding of electron addition at metal oxide/water interfaces, but that they raise as many questions as they answer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, for the first time, the band edges of metal oxide semiconducors can be determined with a high degree of confidence.
electron transfer at the band edges of metal oxide semicondutors is not a simple, well-defined process, as it is often assumed to be.
the electrochemical band edges for metal oxides are not determined solely by the intrinsic properties of the semiconductor but rather are strongly affected by the nature of the electrolyte solution.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the absence of specific chemical interactions, electron addition at metal oxide semiconductive surfaces is accompanied by proton uptake.
, in the case of nanocrystallite metal oxide semicondctors, band edge energetics can be controlled chemically, and the band edge can be pinned at an arbitrary position in the electrochemical cell.
the electrochemical behavior of semiconductors is much more complex than is generally appreciated.
